title: "I'm Sad in the Classroom, and I'm Sad in the Dorm Too" | "Ten Years" ⑥
excerpt: "I feel wronged, because I didn't cause this — and it's still on me to deal with."
body:
"I feel wronged, because I didn't cause this — and it's still on me to deal with."

**A week ago, on a Wednesday afternoon, Chen Yimo's mother, Li Ling, put down her work and drove back from Wenchuan county, 70 kilometers away, to their home in Dujiangyan, to blow out birthday candles with her daughter. "Leave it all to time — growing up is a process," Li Ling said.**

**That day Chen Yimo turned 18.**

**In 2008, Chen Yimo was a first-grader at Yingxiu Primary School, and the classmate everyone envied. Unlike the other left-behind children there, she had both parents at the school — both were teachers — and had never been apart from them.**

**In her memory, that was the one time her life was whole.**

**On May 12, 2008, Chen Yimo lost her father in the earthquake. Her hand, crushed too long under the rubble, died of tissue necrosis.**

**She was one of only five children in her class who lived.**

**She has had several operations since. The first came four days after the earthquake, a decompression surgery to see whether the hand could be saved; she was eight. The second confirmed it could not, and the hand was amputated. The most recent was because she is still growing: new bone kept pushing through her skin and had to be filed down. "I don't want to remember that time again. I don't want her to have another operation. I don't want to watch her hurt again," Li Ling said.**

**The pain in her body has stopped for now. What came next was the pain in her mind.**

**After the earthquake, Chen Yimo transferred from Yingxiu Primary School to Dujiangyan Youai School, where she spent her primary and middle school years. At its peak the school had 140 students left disabled by the earthquake, and Chen Yimo was taken in without judgment.**

**For high school she tested into Dujiangyan No. 1 High School, a provincial key school in Sichuan. Among several thousand able-bodied students, she felt out of place.**

**"Students in other classes said she doesn't have a hand, and she minds very much what people say. Wherever she goes she feels as if someone is talking about her — there's a shadow in her head." Once her daughter started high school, this became the problem Li Ling had to face every weekend.**

**Every Sunday night, Chen Yimo resisted going back to school. Li Ling would talk her round and her mood would lift a little, but by the next weekend at home she was back where she started. "Once I'm at school, I snap back into my old self," Chen Yimo said. Even in class she can't concentrate. "I'm sad in the classroom, and I'm sad in the dorm too."**

**Family and friends are inside the line Chen Yimo draws around herself. Past that line she refuses contact with the outside world and refuses to go out, as if everyone on the street would point and stare. "She just wants to shut herself in at home," is how Li Ling described her daughter's recent state.**

**Since high school began, several forces have pulled at Chen Yimo at once: shame about her body, adolescence, the pressure of the college entrance exam, fear of what's ahead, and the grief for her father that she has never shaken off…**

**At her lowest she has thought about ending the struggle for good. "I really have thought about doing something to end all of this… I think about it every month," Chen Yimo said.**

**To her, her mother's answers can sound heartless. When her disability or her dead father comes up, the comfort her mother offers most often is "there's nothing to be done." It was also the phrase Li Ling used most in our interview, usually followed by a sigh.**

**"This can't be changed, and no one in the world can change it for her — it's something she has to accept... All she can do is face the hard thing. There's no other way… (sighs)."**

**"I tell her this was a natural disaster, there was nothing to be done. At least you're alive — there were dozens of students in your class and only four or five of you are left. You're alive, you can watch the sun come up, see this beautiful world, all these good things."**

**Li Ling won't let her daughter run herself down or sink into self-pity. She believes this is a passage Chen Yimo has to go through, and bear alone.**

**She makes Chen Yimo do most things herself — washing clothes, carrying luggage — to build her confidence, and steps in only when there is no other way.**

**She doesn't plan to keep her daughter under her wing forever. If Chen Yimo can get into a university outside Sichuan, she will back her all the way to go see the wider world.**

**Two years after the earthquake, Li Ling started a new family. Chen Yimo now lives in Dujiangyan with her mother, her stepfather and her younger brother — four of them.**

**On March 10, 2018, introduced by a former Yingxiu Primary School classmate, we met Chen Yimo at a café in downtown Dujiangyan. She wore a loose white long-sleeved T-shirt, her long black hair down.**

**When the interview ended and we walked out of the café, a few strangers came toward us. Chen Yimo pulled her sleeve down without thinking and held the cuff shut in her hand.**

**The whole time, she kept looking straight ahead.**

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20180530230554FKtsWNvqaXDPU0QA.jpg-w600)

In 2008 my mom and my dad were both teachers at Yingxiu Primary School. When the earthquake hit, my mom ran out of the office. My dad died in it — he was on the fifth floor.

After the earthquake, in second grade, I went to Chengdu for chemotherapy. I did one semester at a primary school in Chengdu and then moved to Dujiangyan, and I never went back to Aba prefecture — I've lived in Dujiangyan ever since. My mom thought the teaching in Dujiangyan was a bit better than in Yingxiu.

We'd bought an apartment in Dujiangyan before the earthquake, but we'd always rented it out and never lived in it. After the earthquake we moved in. Later I didn't want to go back to Yingxiu either, because it's a very sad place. Most of the friends I knew went to school in Dujiangyan too. Basically none of us went back.

After primary school I kept in touch with Lin Hao and Chai Zhengdong. Lin Hao comes to Dujiangyan sometimes, and when I'm in Chengdu I go find him. He looks out for me, treats me like a little sister. I think Lin Hao has had more chances than I have, but apart from that there isn't much difference. It doesn't bother me. I'm not envious.

What I think is unfair is the physical part, the injury. Comparing my body with theirs, that I think is unfair. But I don't think the paths their lives took are unfair to me — your fate is in your own hands.

The disability has affected a lot — school, daily life, the future… all of it different from other people. At school I have to work harder; plenty of things are hard, like using a ruler to draw in math class. Daily life is a hassle too. I can do a lot of things myself, but I'm still not like other people, I'm slower than they are.

I've worn a prosthetic hand — I can draw with it. I used to have a powered one, but it had a lot of machinery and batteries inside, so picking things up with it was heavy, and I stopped wearing it.

**Dujiangyan Youai School was formerly Dujiangyan Taipingjie Primary School. After the May 12 earthquake it was rebuilt on a new site, teaching both primary and middle school grades. Zhang Haidi, chairwoman of the China Disabled Persons' Federation, wrote the new name, Youai — "friendship and love" — in her own calligraphy. The school takes in disabled students; of its more than 100 disabled students, 80% were injured and disabled in the earthquake, most of them from Yingxiu, Qingchuan, Pingwu and other areas of Sichuan hit hardest.**

For primary school I was at Youai in Dujiangyan. I think primary school was pretty happy, I didn't think much about any of this. Youai has primary and middle school together, and I was very used to it there. It's a boarding school, and there were other students there who'd been hurt in the earthquake.

Middle school was really good, the classmates were good too. But after I got to high school (she paused, and began to choke up)… I used to think being outgoing was my strong point, but after high school started I found I wasn't outgoing anymore. I'd become sensitive.

Because in high school you're thinking about the future, about what's coming. People would say I'm not like other people, that later on nobody will want to hire me, that others will look down on me, so I have to work harder than everyone else. I don't much like being pitied or felt sorry for. My pride is strong, and I hope I won't let my mom and my family down.

![A young woman's hands](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201805302310300PGbv3xaijgV9uzh.jpg-w600)

I decided in primary school to go the art track. I drew all through primary school, but back then I didn't know there was an art route through the college entrance exam. I learned about the art exam after middle school started, and began studying sketching in eighth grade. I made a lot of progress at sketching — my teacher said I had a feel for it.

My parents and my teachers told me that when it comes to jobs, if someone is at your level, the two of you equally good, and the same company is hiring, they'll look at your individual circumstances, and they'll take him or her, not you. So I have to stand on a platform where there aren't many people — a higher platform, fewer people, more chances.

Every time I hear them say "you're not like other people," I burn, I feel wronged. I know what they're saying is right, but there's a fire inside me. I feel wronged, because I didn't cause this — and it's still on me to deal with.

Actually, right after the earthquake, in 2008, I was in a bad way, but by 2009 things got better. Those years in between I was pretty happy. But these last few years I seem to have slid back. I think it's because I've grown up, I think more, and I've become more and more sensitive.

Now I feel raw a lot of the time. My temper isn't good, I'm thin-skinned, easy to break, and it takes a long time to feel better. I wasn't like this as a child. The older I get the more easily I break. As a child I wasn't afraid of setbacks; grown up, I've started to be afraid.

Some people on the street look at me strangely. Not just now — it's always been like that. I used to think it was nothing, but now that I'm older I mind how I look, so it gets to me. It really gets to me.

I've told my mom about it, but she says there's nothing she can do either. "That's how you are. People looking at you is only curiosity. You can't stop people looking."

I haven't seen a therapist. My mom says the mind mainly comes down to yourself — if you haven't worked it out for yourself, if you're lying on the ground and don't want to get up, nobody who pulls at you can pull you up. So it still comes down to you.

**Once her daughter started high school, Li Ling often talked to her homeroom teacher, to make sure the students in that class would understand Chen Yimo and not order her around. She could not make the rest of the school follow suit. "There are so many students at that school, thousands of them — how am I supposed to talk to them all? And out in society there will be even more, hundreds of millions. I can't go and say hello to every one of them. Is that possible? You can't change other people, you can only change yourself," Li Ling said.**

**Lately, Chen Yimo's situation has improved. She's joined an art prep class, which lets her step out of ordinary high school life for a while; now she only has to deal with a dozen or so other art students around her. Her anxiety has dropped sharply, and she asks to come home less often.**

**Getting into the art class was itself a sorting. The tuition is high, and several classmates who had planned to train alongside Chen Yimo were shut out because their families couldn't afford it. Li Ling isn't especially well-off, but she tries to clear away whatever obstacle is in front of her daughter — that much she can do something about. "In April alone I paid close to 30,000 yuan. I try to find a way… but she has no idea how hard that money is to come by," Li Ling said.**

**Chen Yimo wants to get into the Central Academy of Fine Arts and work in design after she graduates. Fashion design is out, because it means cutting fabric by hand, so she has set her sights on art direction for film, where all the work can be done on a computer. She hopes that one day her name will be in the credits that roll after a film ends.**

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20180530231452Zqr8bOhTXWHKnEUQ.jpg-w600)

For high school I'm at Dujiangyan No. 1, and I thought it would be about the same as middle school. Most students at Youai School were able-bodied, but over 100 had disabilities, so I was relaxed about it there — plenty of people knew.

At Dujiangyan No. 1, basically everyone is normal.

Take the morning group run in high school. I usually don't take part, because there are movements I can't do, but inside I still want to join in. After high school started it began to bother me, because suddenly there were so many people around. At first I did the between-class exercises too, but a bunch of people around me kept staring at me strangely, so after that I stopped. Now during exercise time I stay in the classroom.

I complain to my mom about it, and all she says is: "There's nothing to be done, you just have to get used to it." She doesn't have a way either.

Over these 10 years I've grown up a bit. When I was small I liked to cry and make a scene, I felt the world revolved around me, but it isn't like that in high school — it's more about giving way and putting yourself in someone else's place.

Before, maybe because I was hurt, everyone ached for me. Nobody said a harsh word to me as a child. My mom, the family, hardly ever scolded me; sometimes they'd say a few words and let it go. Now in high school there are so many people, so many classmates, not like middle school where there were only so many. A single grade in high school has several hundred people, close to 1,000, and you meet all kinds of different people. Once there are that many people, it turns out you're not the center.

Back in middle school I only hoped to get into high school. I didn't think about the college entrance exam, the pressure wasn't that heavy, my grades were above average. Our grade had two classes, over 90 students, and I ranked around 20th to 30th. In one diagnostic exam across Dujiangyan, more than 5,000 students, I came somewhere past 1,000th. At Dujiangyan No. 1, a provincial key school, where I've been over a year now, the pressure is far greater than in middle school.

Even though all my mom says is that she hopes I'll finish school and do something good with my life, I put more pressure on myself too. I badly want to get into a good university and not let them down.

I used to think getting into college was easy, and when I first started high school I wanted to have fun, but once I sat the exams I saw it wasn't like that. My grades dropped hard in the first semester of tenth grade. In the first semester of eleventh grade I worked and they came back up. My mom would reason with me; at first I found it irritating, but afterwards I thought about it and she was right — getting into college isn't as simple as I thought.

My homeroom teacher talked to me a few times too, hoping I'd try harder, because right after I started high school my state of mind was terrible. I was listless, my grades were sliding badly, I didn't want to study, I'd more or less given up on myself.

She told me: "If you don't respect yourself, who else is going to respect you?"

**"Whether it's work or people, I feel like I can get along with everyone very well — so why is it only with her that it's like this?" Li Ling said, baffled by how she and her daughter get along.**

**Chen Yimo often loses her temper at her, and sometimes takes it out on Li Ling's mother — her own grandmother. Li Ling sounds angry when she describes it: "That's my own mother. In my whole life I've never sworn at her or talked back to her once. How can you do that?"**

**Most of the time, Li Ling understands her daughter's irritability and helplessness at this age. She usually works the feelings out herself and makes peace with her daughter quickly.**

**But when Chen Yimo has said, more than once, that she wants to end it all, fear takes hold of Li Ling's anger. She can't let it go, and she can't understand it: "I think, everyone around you, family and friends, loves you so much — why would you have thoughts like that?"**

**Every one of these fierce arguments ends with cruel words on both sides and both of them in tears.**

**The arguing lets out Chen Yimo's fear of being unsafe. When her mother tells her that she insists on coming home from 70 kilometers away every Friday just to cook her favorite dishes, and keeps saying how much she loves her, Chen Yimo sees for a moment that she isn't alone, and that there's a reason to keep living.**

**In one way Li Ling can understand her daughter's pain, because she too lost her father young. In another way she can't, because she got through everything on her own and made it to university — so why can't her daughter?**

**When we told Li Ling that her daughter thinks her mother is the stronger of the two, Li Ling was surprised, and couldn't hide her excitement: "That's how she sees me? That's good. I thought she saw me as someone who's good to her but... doesn't understand her."**

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20180530232140J7txQzZCbES2aIv4.jpg-w600)

My mom is stronger, stronger than me. From May to August after the earthquake, she cried her heart out. For years after the earthquake she cried easily. Back in middle school, when she heard me say something upsetting, she'd often go hide in her room and cry.

I used to tell her I'm not like other people, the gap is huge, I didn't even want to go on living, I really felt I couldn't survive. My mood would crash all at once, my feelings weren't steady. She'd be very upset too, but she wouldn't cry in front of me — she'd lecture me and be upset by herself afterwards.

I think the main thing is that my pride is strong, and I don't like sympathy, I don't like being looked down on. Some things just make me burn.

I really have thought about not wanting to live. When my mood is bad I think about trying it (suicide). It's happened more in high school — in high school I'm mostly in a low state, and I board at the school.

I'm sad in the classroom, and I'm sad in the dorm too.

I really have thought about doing something to end all of this. I haven't done it, but I've wanted to. I think about it every month. I've told my mom this. One time she cried and told me that if I died, she'd die too.

Every time my mom and I finish fighting, my mood is a little better, because once it's out I can tell she and the others are worried about me, and that makes me feel better.

When I fight with a classmate over something, it just leaves me in a bad mood, but fighting with my mom is a release. After we fight we're both gentle with each other, and we don't bring it up again — we act as if it never happened.

Before the fight I feel low about myself and very unsafe, but after we fight, when my mom says, "You go and die and I'll die too, whatever you do I'll do," I feel there's still someone worrying about me.

Part of me wants to see a therapist and part of me doesn't. I want to because they might make me feel better; I don't want to because I feel that after hearing all of it, after a while I'll go back to how I was.

My mom married later, and in 2011 she had a son, so we became a new family, where before it was just the two of us. I think it's about the same for me whether we have a new family or not, because I don't see much of him. With (my stepfather) I'm not especially warm and not especially distant. I think he's good to me, but I always feel he isn't my birth father, so there's a barrier and a distance.

There's always a barrier. I can't let go.

When my mom first started seeing him I resisted a little, but later they told me that having someone to share the load would make things easier for her.

**By Li Ling's account, the stepfather never plays favorites — a share for the younger brother, a share for the older sister, both treated the same — and he even looks after the family of Chen Yimo's dead father.**

**But toward this man she calls "Dad Zhang," Chen Yimo has always had a knot in her.**

**When there's friction with Chen Yimo, "Dad Zhang" talks to her over WeChat, showing Li Ling what he plans to write before he sends it. "He's afraid of hurting you too, you know?" Li Ling said. "I told her, if your birth father were here he'd probably have slapped you across the face by now, but he didn't. When he's angry he doesn't shout at you — he calms down first and then talks to you."**

**Li Ling knows the unease and anxiety her daughter feels also happen in families with children the same age; it's only that her daughter's circumstances make the friction escalate faster. "What I really long for is the day she understands… I look forward to that day."**

**Near the end of the interview, we finally put "the earthquake" and "father" to Chen Yimo directly.**

**"The time right after the earthquake — that was when you were in the most pain, wasn't it?"**

**"I'm in a lot of pain now too."**

**"When did you accept that your father is gone?"**

**"I never have."**

I've never accepted family bringing up my father either. Avoidance, I suppose — I can't stand to hear it. Sometimes my mom talks about my dad as he was. Before the earthquake we weren't well off, but every year on my birthday my dad bought me a cake. He spoiled me a bit, though he was strict about school. Now my mom will say: "If your dad were still here and saw you on your phone all day like this, he'd be furious."

That makes me burn. I feel you can say whatever you like, just don't drag my dad into it.

My dad shaped the kind of person I am. He taught me to be generous, not petty. I used to have Barbie dolls I loved and didn't want anyone touching. Once a friend came over and touched my dolls, and I didn't want them touched, and my dad got very angry — he even hit me for it — telling me not to be petty, not to be selfish, that toys are for playing with and you have to know how to share.

So now I like sharing, giving my things away.

Even now, when people bring up my dad, I still can't take it, it still makes me burn.

There's one person missing from my life.

**As we were about to end our conversation with Li Ling, she suddenly added one last thing over the phone: "Honestly, the one I ache for most is her. Sometimes when I think of her it's like a needle going into my heart. Who wants their own child to end up like this?"**

At the request of the interview subjects, Li Ling and Chen Yimo are pseudonyms.

The cover image and unlabeled inline images are from [Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/photos/knK5UcINLuM)
